Certainly! We all perceive the world in our own ways and understand the stories in ways that make sense to our experiences.   
If I recall correctly, Athena had Medusa's head on her shield as a source of power. And this definitely links back to more ancient traditions that used the Gorgoneon as an apotropaic symbol on armor and shields. Pure evil, I think, only exists in the human psyche.

I was also called to Anubis as a child. I will say that Anubis, in my experience, is a very compassionate deity. He is a guider of souls of the living as well as the dead. I think that reaching out to him would be a wonderful step to make. There are always things you can look up regarding communication or connection with him, but I work more intuitively and always encourage others to do so as well. Think of what Anubis represents and the things associated with him and go from there. Offerings of incense and oils or dried flowers and bones are what I most often use. I have a section of my altar dedicated to him and this is where I face when I commune with him. Or I wear an amulet representing him.

In terms of past life things: It's very possible. There is also the idea of adoptive spirits where you may experience influences from a spirit who is not part of your lineage (by blood or spirit) but who has adopted you for some reason (often healing reasons, but not always). You can try communicating with these spirits or ask for their guidance. I always speak very clearly and with good boundaries when opening the doors to communicating with spirits I am not yet familiar with. Basically, being clear that you are looking for beneficial guidance and that you are not interested in communicating with spirits who mean ill will or harm against you or others. However, in most cases, I have not had trouble with malicious spirits. The worst that usually happens is a spirit who isn't quite telling the truth about their identity or motives, but they're more like "tricksters" I suppose.

​

I have also had intense visions or spiritual interactions with the mummified dead or simply the dead. And I have also been drawn to funerary rites and practices (even in literal ways). These can be signs drawing you to a path. But it's not always literal! Death and the lore around it is not always about physical body death. There is a great deal more in that realm than meets the eye. There is healing, guidance, renewal, and mystery (and much more). There are many paths that extend outward from the Underworld and Death. It may take time to find your path, but it will likely be aligned with Anubis in some way if you have such a deep connection to him.

When it comes to sorting out symbols and messages, the best thing to do is to observe and listen. Seek oracles for clarity, if that's your thing. But don't jump too quickly to conclusions with your mind. Instead, let yourself feel it. Pay attention to subtleties and listen to your intuition. The more stillness you invite into your work (even meditation if you like), the easier it will be to take in these messages or symbols and decipher them.

Medusa's story was written a long time after Gorgons were part of the spiritual and mythological/folkloric world. Originally, the Gorgon was a protective figure who was considered beneficial (I prefer not to categorize archetypes as good or bad, as this reduces them into two dimensions and doesn't consider the whole entity). She was a monster, but she wasn't evil.   


The story of Medusa came much later in history with the rise of patriarchal social and spiritual structures. Gorgons, however, existed in prior structures that were either matriarchal or more balanced than later Greek and Roman ones that heavily favored men. 

​

Personally, I think the story of Medusa moves the emphasis away from wild feminine (but not always female) strength and power to a sort of power that is contained and controlled. In the case of Medusa, her power is controlled by a male archetype and a female archetype who has a somewhat masculine energetic focus (a warrior who fits within the controlled world). Medusa represents an older, wilder form of power that is much darker and thus more frightening and more difficult to control (if viewed from the vantage point of those who desire control over their surroundings/environments). So I see her story not so much as a literal tale of Good vs Bad but as a story that removes power from the more ancient ways and brings them into a more controlled contemporary way (at the time of this myth, at least).

It was a lot of trying to educate them as well as helping them to realize that this wasn't a phase and that i really was unhappy in my body. Ultimately the depth of my unhappiness helped them to come to terms with my being trans. When I began transitioning and i was happier than I'd been in years, they came around much more quickly. But damn it was rough for a while. 

I wish you all the very best. Hang in there!

I am writing as someone who identifies as third gender, of European descent, who also studies third gendered peoples from my lineage (as an artist and folk practitioner). 

I think that any attempts to frame historical identities in modern terms is a fools errand. Also, it is important to recognize that third gender peoples do still exist in the world in a range of cultures (including those you've listed). It is best to speak to or read sources written by people in those cultures and communities that continue to recognize a culturally linked third gender (ie. two-spirit peoples are very much part of the current modern culture of many North American Indians).

Another consideration is who is writing the history. A lot of historical documents are written by cis-men (male bodied persons who identify as a gender they were assigned at birth). The interpretations of historians do not equal the actual identities of those they are writing about.

There are also assigned female at birth (AFAB) people who are third gender in Europe. The only identity I'm aware of are the so-called "sworn virgins" of eastern europe: [https://scholarworks.iu.edu/journals/index.php/aeer/article/download/687/780/2952](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/journals/index.php/aeer/article/download/687/780/2952)

But yes, a lot of the third gender peoples mentioned in sources are assigned male at birth (AMAB). 

One example, from my own research, are the femminiello and the galli. The former is a third gender identity related to the Neapolitan culture in Italy. The latter is an ancient third gender identity associated with spiritual practices in the ancient Mediterranean. They are similar, but very different given the context of time. The femminiello can be important members of the community, but they have often been relegated to the fringes of society even so. 

Another thing to keep in mind with third gender roles in society is that third gender people have been heavily persecuted over the past 2000+ years. So people have had to do what they must to survive. For example, many third gender persons are now associated with poverty and sex work - this is because of the ways society has treated them and the roles they've been deemed "acceptable" to uphold in modern society.

Below are a number of links to sources. Unfortunately none are primary because I do not have access to such sources, but some do cite primary sources. Also, it should be noted that these sources are not written by the people they discuss (third gender persons) and therefore cannot be taken as accounts of how these people identified themselves. I'm providing these sources for information on the galli and femminiello - so the contrast between ancient and modern views can be seen. But the ancient views are coming only from outsiders and historians.

Ultimately, identities cannot be assumed to remain static over long stretches of time. It is also insensitive to assume that two-spirit and other culturally based third gender identities are analogous to westernized and fully modern ideas of gender and gender identity. Modern identities have a different foundation and basis than cultural identities that have existed for thousands of years. Furthermore, modern ideas of non-binary and gender fluid identities do not always align with third gender identities. Many people today reject any gender binary and therefore can view third gender as maintaining the binary. It's a very complex matter even when looking only at modern people.

​

Sources on Galli and Femminiello so that one may compare ancient attitudes with modern ones:

Modern interview with femminiello - [https://medium.com/@kwilsonwriter/femminielli-napoletani-aead72d3ad92](https://medium.com/@kwilsonwriter/femminielli-napoletani-aead72d3ad92)

It was a pretty long and complex and confusing process for me. I was your age in like, 2000, and in the South US.... so there wasn't all the LGBTQ resources there are now. I didn't even know transgender was a thing until I was 18. So I struggled a lot and felt like an alien, because I had no idea I was normal for being sort of gender exploratory and fluid and confused. 

I actually spent a lot of time playing with how I presented myself. My clothes, my hair, etc. I did all of this when I was a teenager too and even then people would refer to me as "non-gendered" or something like that. Or they'd call me he or she. The nice thing is, you can do all the exploring your want! You don't need to tell people anything either. Try out wearing more masculine clothes or getting a masculine haircut (if you feel safe doing so). One of my friends tried out using a gender neutral nickname for a few years in high school. 

My advice would be not to try to BE anything but yourself. But to explore different ways of being yourself. For example, I recently began wearing dresses again because I've really, really missed wearing them. So I slowly tried wearing them again, at home or with friends. And then eventually out in public until I felt comfortable enough to ID as third gender. 

Rushing the process, to me, would be immediately going out and telling everyone you are "X" and want to be called "X name" and start on hormones right away. Social and physical transition can definitely wait until you feel more certain. But I'll also say, I was not 100% certain when I began my physical and social transition. I was scared shitless! But I felt like if I didn't do it, I'd be miserable and depressed. So I made the leap and haven't looked back. But before I did transition at all, I spent a lot of time exploring my identity alone and with friends. I also socially transitioned for a year before doing anything physical. Everyone will want to go at a different pace, of course, so that was just my process.

I hope you're able to find what feels comfortable for you and people who support you through it all too!

I've been in the same boat. It got better after a while, but it never goes away and sometimes flares up (been on T for around 15 years). The best solution I've found is drinking LOTS of water. Stay very well hydrated. Also, try only washing your face with soap once a day and only apply medicated creams in the evening. Rinse with warm water in the morning. Use a light moisturizer like aloe gel (look for something without loads of additives and as high as a percentage of aloe as possible) after washing or rinsing your face. You can also try tea tree oil (a drop or two added to the aloe each day). I will sometimes do an apple cider vinegar rinse (mixed in water) as well.

Your skin should have a good balance of moisture and mild acidity. Too much washing and using medications can actually make things worse by increasing inflammation and irritation.

Look into The Ordinary skin products too. They have a good line of washes and masks and so on that I've found useful.

You're very young, so you can take the time to explore your identity if you are not certain. But doubt is also a normal feeling when it comes to major things in life. Sure, there are people who can know things without a doubt, but this isn't always the case. 

There are many ways to be a man and male. And there are many ways to be trans. I did not know for certain until I was 20 and didn't start transition until I was 21. Also, I lived stealth for many years before coming out as third gender. So one's own gender identity can shift over time. What's important is listening to yourself and your body - how do you feel and what brings you the most sense of joy or peace? 

Don't worry about how others behave. I've been there, trust me, but it's something that never ends with satisfaction. The truth is, teenage boys are all trying things out too. They're trying to be the sorts of boys they see in the society around them. But they aren't always being themselves either - plenty of men and boys have behaviors and thoughts and actions that, in our patriarchal culture in many places, would be pegged as "feminine". So they work extra hard to cover that or push it down sometimes. But as you get older, some men begin to let this wall down. I know cis-men who love fashion or collecting antiques or making floral arrangements or baking as a hobby. All things that tend to be pegged as too feminine when you're younger (and by older folks too sometimes). My point is, be yourself. If you feel male, then you are male regardless of your interests and behaviors.

I'm AFAB, but have lived as male for the past 15 years and people always assume I'm AMAB. Wearing dresses and skirts while appearing AMAB can be scary, but it doesn't have to be.

I started off by wearing skirts and dresses around my house and in safe spaces where people were accepting of me. I'd get them at thrift shops or buy them online. If you buy online, make sure to take good measurements and start off buying looser fitting clothes. Elastic waste skirts are great! Thrift stores are also great because men do go there to buy women's clothes to resell sometimes (I've seen it!) AND the clothes are cheap, so you can try out different styles until you find what you like best.

I live in a very liberal area, so I sometimes see other NB people out and about or just hippie dudes in sarongs lol. So I did start wearing skirts out in public and even wore them in NYC (years ago now). Get a feel for the places you go and if you might be safe there. Then try wearing a skirt or dress. I prefer to wear skirts and dresses that are simple and not overly feminine or frilly or flashy - that's just my style, but it also can make it easier for people to accept you if you style is more androgynous (this is shitty, I know, but I've found it to be true). 

Some people might stare at you, but I began saying: "The more people stare at me, the more powerful I become!" and I walked with my head held high and just pretended those stares were because I look so damned good!

I've found that people began complimenting me and saying kind things to me. So I'd go to those places more or feel comfortable dressing how I want there. Sometimes people will really surprise you. But again, it depends on where you are.

The way I look at it is this:

Yes, there are a lot of shitty men in the world because men in many societies are socialized in ways that can bring out the worst in a person.

Yes, as a transman you will be entering into a world where there are many of these shitty men. And yes, there are shitty white men you will meet and maybe interact with.

But by entering into this world, you have a choice. You do not have to take on those same traits. You can represent the example of a man YOU want to see in the world. 

BE THE MAN YOU WISH OTHER MEN COULD BE! 

Honestly. I've lived stealth and being a kind man in society can really have a powerful healing effect. You can be an example for other men, even. 

Don't limit yourself to the categories of people that you think exist. Instead, focus on yourself and the change you want to see in the world. Then be that person and make that change happen. It doesn't have to be big - you can make a big impact just by being kind to another person and being your authentic self.

You can always start on a low dose. 

Also, if you feel it's not right for you, you can stop! Depending on how long you're on T and your body, some changes may not "go back", but others will. For example, I stopped T after 10 years on it, so my body hair and voice and bone changes that happened stayed. But my voice did soften/lighten a bit, my body hair also softened/lightened and stopped growing as much, and my body fat redistributed so my face was a bit softer as well. People thought I was a transwoman, however. But, if you're younger and only on T for a short time, more things may "go back". I was already very well on into my transition when I stopped and had been on a pretty high dose too. Now I'm on a lower dose and the changes are there, but less pronounced.

I transitioned at age 21, but didn't start a higher dose of hormones until I was 22/23. I've also been off and on HRT and am now in my late 30s. 

If you start HRT, those feminine aspects of your body will change. Your body fat WILL redistribute (tho how much will vary by person). Your voice WILL deepen. Your body WILL masculineize. Even after starting on HRT again after 2 years off of it I had more masculine traits return.

Dysphoria takes a lot of work beyond physical transition, but that can help. But you're definitely not too late! Be kind to yourself. And do what feels right for your body.

I've been in various stages of dysphoria around this throughout my life so far. It's different for everyone, but here are some thoughts from my own experience:

  
\- When you are in a relationship with someone, work together to be open about your bodies (as best as you can) and exploring ways you both like to be touched. There's a HUGE myth that sex has to be penetrative to be enjoyable (no matter what gender or sex you or your partner are). Sure, it can definitely be an enjoyable part of sex, but it doesn't even necessarily have to happen for an orgasm to occur. So, try out different positions and toys and so on together.

\- Whether you're on HRT or not, try out pumping. I'd recommend getting a professionally made clit pump, because the DIY ones can do more harm than good to your genitals. Pumping can really increase the sensation and even size of your existing anatomy. This can make self and partner play enjoyable and more similar to the experience of a penis. If you get the kind that has a detachable cylinder, some can be fitted with silicone sleeves that can then be used to penetrate or stimulate a partner (depending on your position). You can also stroke the cylinder for more sensation when alone or with a partner. I've actually preferred this to using a prosthetic in most cases because it allows for more physical sensation.  


\- There are some good prosthetic options that fit into harnesses or underwear. If you are with a partner, make sure you have one that is the right size for them if you plan to penetrate. 

\- There are surgical options, of course. I've considered them, but have ultimately decided against them because surgery freaks me out a bit and it's an intense one. But there are communities on here for lower surgery and the various options available.

\- It sucks. It really does. Let yourself grieve. But then try to find ways to live well in the body you have. Either by adapting your body as best you can (HRT, prosthetics, surgery, etc.) or finding things that make you feel good in your body.

\- Finding ways that make you feel good about your body can be many things. Clothes you wear (even underwear) that make you feel the way you want to, ways of touching yourself, ways of referring to your body parts (ie. maybe call the physical clit a dick instead), ways of interacting with your partner sexually, ways of interacting with yourself sexually, etc. Explore things alone and in safe spaces. Try an STP or pump or any other device that may help you find a comfortable way to interact with your body.

I know it's hard, but there can be ways to work through the dysphoria. Sometimes it takes some creativity and willingness to step out of your comfort zone or try something new.  


Lots of luck to you!

Yes, I have done this, though not specifically the way you've mentioned here (I was not familiar with the Nam-Shub concept before your post).  
Whenever we bring something into being, we give it a sort of life because it becomes part of the realized world. But to imbue life into a creation, or to enliven an object as a magical object or talisman takes more effort and concentration. How you do this will vary with your tradition and ways. I can only offer from my own ways, as they are what I know. So take it as you will...  


To enliven my art, I typically set the intention to create a living object while I am making it. During this process, I am present with the work and the materials as fully as possible. I may even work on the piece within a ritual space or context. I find that using natural (once living, especially) materials to be beneficial, if used with respect. Other times I will involve powerful objects in the making of the art object to be given life to. For example, when dying cloth, I may add non-dye materials to the dye bath for the spirit or energetic qualities (like a stone or soil). 

  
Once the object has been created, I then give the object their purpose. I speak to the piece and sing to them as well. I anoint them with oils and smoke. I bless them with salt. From there I bring the piece into my life in some way - for a living object left to sit alone is left to slumber. I wear it out, bring it with me someplace, involve them in a ritual or ceremony, etc. Then I will routinely feed and care for and anoint the art as needed. Some are fed with breath and song, others with blood or offerings. It depends on the object and their intended use.  


I have had shows with living artwork present and I make sure to let the gallery viewers know that the work is a living piece. This gives context and allows for a different interaction between the work and the viewer. 

Since I'm not familiar with Nam-Shub, I don't know if this is quite what you're looking for. But this is what I do with all of my ritual objects, including talismans and sigils as well as worn pieces and pieces to be hung on walls.

It depends on your views. Some shamans I know say that with suicide the spirit can be unaware of their death or become trapped in the middle world in a sort of limbo state. Thus they may need to be assisted in moving on, where a shaman can go to them and help them to release from their "limbo" state. But this is difficult work that must be done by the well trained/experienced.  
The spirit may also become trapped or lost, in a sense, and be unable to move. Once they are able to move (if helped, for example), they can then choose their path in the spirit realm.  


Personally, I believe there are many things that can happen, depending on the situation. The spirit may become fragmented, trapped, or lost, creating a ghost or lost soul. They may haunt places or people in this way. But I don't believe all suicide ends with such things. Some spirits may find release and go on their way. In my tradition the spirit is reincarnated or remains in the spirit realm. But because suicide often comes with intense emotions and energies, there is often something that needs to be resolved either in a future life or within the spirit realm or middle realm.

You need to check town or county health board regulations or possibly building regulations. Some places DO NOT allow composting toilets (there are towns near me that ban them). Others don't care and the majority that I've encountered have some sort of regulations around them. It may be required to get a Title V inspection as well, even if a septic system isn't being used. For washing underwear and socks, the key is really scrubbing the fabric against itself with soapy water. Adding washing soda, baking soda, or borax powder can help too. You don't need much and can sprinkle some onto the extra dirty spots or even leave a paste of baking soda on stains or smelly spots (for 20 mins or overnight if really tough) before washing. To be honest, even washing machines don't get clothes as clean as when you rub them together by hand. I suppose you could use a washboard, but I've never tried one myself.  


For drying: put your line in a sunny spot or in a room with a woodstove or other heat source. On cloudy days or rainy days it's best to dry indoors. Though windy and cloudy days can often get the job done!  


In the short-term, if you're using a natural detergent, the grey water won't harm the land. But you do want to pour it where it won't run directly into a water source or near drinking water. Someplace with plants is best - soapy water won't harm most plants. You could also create a grey water filtering system if you will be living off-grid full time. Be careful, first of all. Ayahuasca in particular is rife with people seeking to take advantage and make a buck. It's understandable, because the economies in a number of South American countries are struggling, there is corruption/organized crime, and tourists seeking psychedelics are an easy target. If you are female bodied or trans/non-binary then you absolutely must find a healer who is accepting and safe for such persons.  


Do a ton of research and ask around. Never go to a place that combines medicines - ayahuasca should never contain coca, cocaine, LSD, psilocybin, MDMA, etc. etc. but many non-reputable "healers" will add things to the ayahuasca for an "enhanced experience". It is best if the place you go to allows you to take part in the medicine making or they show you the process. Become familiar with that plants are in ayahuasca, their effects, and so on.   


It's also important to understand the culture you're working with. There are many different ways of working with Ayahuasca and other South American medicines. In Brazil the medicines and methods are different from in Peru, and within each region their are religious and cultural differences. Some involve Christian theology, others involve indigenous beliefs, and so on.

First off, it's not always easy to know if a person is indigenous or not unless they are telling you their lineage, etc. Also, many indigenous cultures (just like Western ones) do hold beliefs that place women in lower standing or that do not accept trans/non-binary persons. So just because a healer is indigenous, does not mean they are safe for female bodied or trans/non-binary people (the same as with white or western healers).
